title: Hotset Transitions and Bandwidth Coupling — Sprint Log
content:
Summary:

Notes from a short sprint investigating a recurring tail-latency and throughput dip when multiple model families (chat-style long-context and short single-turn generators) run concurrently on the same host. Hypothesis: shifting hotsets across models creates memory-bandwidth coupling that degrades KV cache residency and causes NVMe paging bursts. This doc captures instrumentation, quick repros, measured signals, and candidate mitigations we want to prototype.

Context and motivation:
- Production saw repeated 99th percentile token latency spikes when customer workload mixes long-chat sessions (high KV reuse) and short-high-qps calls (low reuse but many cold KV lookups).
- Previous root-cause threads touched on eviction hysteresis and general prefetching, but we lacked a single-run experiment showing bandwidth coupling across banks and its effect on KV residency.
- This sprint tried to isolate hotset movement across model families and measure: KV reuse rate, DRAM read bandwidth per-channel, PCIe/NVMe request bursts, and cold-page read tail latency.

Experiment design (fast repro):
1) Two synthetic workloads launched on same GPU host: 
   - Worker A: long-context chat model emulator (seqlen 4096, 80% prefix reuse, occasional long KV access patterns).
   - Worker B: short-req generator (seqlen 512, 5% reuse, high arrival rate).
2) Run a 30m baseline with just Worker A to warm KV. Capture residency map (sampled fingerprints), per-request KV hit/miss, and DRAM bandwidth (nvprof / platform PMU counters).
3) Bring up Worker B ramp (0 -> target QPS over 2m). Continue sampling.
4) Repeat with different affinities: colocated on same GPU instance, colocated on same host different GPU, isolated (separate host).

Instrumentation notes (tools and counters used):
- Kernel-level: perf counters for memory controller read bandwidth per-channel (IMC counters), DRAM reads/write counters.
- CUDA/NVML: nvmlDeviceGetMemoryInfo + nvmlDeviceGetPciThroughputCounters sampled every 500ms.
- Runtime: custom KV telemetry: per-request (sampled 1/100) records: prefix_len, kv_hits, kv_miss_reason (evicted, never-loaded), load_latency_ms.
- NVMe: fio trace + iostat (per-namespace), and sampled NVMe admin queue latency via smartctl logs.
- Tracing: zipkin spans for request lifecycle with tags for model_family and kv_cache_tag (hot/windows id).

Key observations (raw):
- Baseline (Worker A only): KV hit-rate ~82% for warm prefixes. DRAM read BW ~60GB/s (host has 96GB/s peak on these cards' channels combined). 99p token latency stable ~18ms.
- When Worker B ramps: sudden drop in observed KV hit-rate to ~57% within 90s of ramp; this correlates with DRAM BW spikes to 92–98GB/s sustained for 30–120s windows.
- NVMe read bursts: average NVMe read latency moved from ~2.1ms (baseline) to 8–12ms during bursts; queue depth increased as runtime moved to spillback reads.
- Affinity effect: colocating both workloads on the same GPU produced the worst coupling (largest hit-rate drop). Co-located different GPUs on same host still produced a measurable hit-rate drop but smaller; separated hosts eliminated the regression.

Deeper probes: what is moving the hotset?
- Fingerprinting shows the hotset from Worker A is relatively stable but when Worker B arrives we see increased churn: top-10% most-reused keys by Worker A get evicted and reloaded repeatedly.
- Eviction causes traced back to pressure from Worker B’s cold misses that force background readbacks and eviction cycles; but primary immediate cause of user-visible tail is delayed reload latency driven by memory-channel saturation.

Hypothesis (refined):
- Not purely an eviction-policy bug. The root is bandwidth coupling: when Worker B issues many unique KV reads, the resulting DRAM/PCIe/NVMe activity saturates shared memory channels and I/O, increasing the latency of reloading evicted pages for Worker A. This creates a feedback loop: A's misses increase, more reloads, more bandwidth usage.

Microbenchmarks and numbers (selected):
- Synthetic cold-read microbenchmark: reading 8KB pages, sequential vs random: random 99p latency increases by 3.8x when DRAM BW above 85GB/s.
- Prefetch vs no-prefetch: enabling conservative prefetch for Worker A reduced its 99p latency from 40ms -> 24ms during mixed run, but increased overall network/IO footprint (so global BW slightly up).
- Bank-localized pinning test: pinning Worker A’s KV to a subset of banks (via allocator hinting) reduced observed BW overlap by ~18% and improved hit-rate by ~6 points.

Operational signals to detect this in prod quickly:
- Correlated jumps: host-level DRAM BW spike + drop in KV hit-rate + NVMe read-latency rise.
- Cross-GPU coupling: different GPU processes on same host with simultaneous increase in miss rates suggest shared-channel coupling.
- Request-level: sudden increase in "kv_miss_reason=evicted" combined with elevated load_latency_ms.

Candidate mitigations (prioritized):
1) Soft isolation windows (short-term): when a tenant induces sustained unique-read rate > threshold, throttle its KV prefetch/backfill concurrency and rate-limit background NVMe readbacks. Quick to implement at runtime admission control.
2) Bank-aware resident allocation: allocate resident KV shards with bank/IMC-awareness to minimize cross-tenant channel overlap. Requires runtime allocator and possible kernel/hw hints.
3) Adaptive prefetch tuning: decrease aggressive prefetch for low-reuse families during mixed workloads and increase for high-reuse models; combine with model-family tagging.
4) Sibling-run placement policy: prefer placing high-unique-read workloads on different hosts or different memory domains when the hotset overlap risk is high. Could be orchestrator-level scheduling rule.
5) Eviction prioritization with writeback smoothing: when evicting, shape background reads to avoid transients (burst smoothing).

Quick prototype we built this sprint:
- Implemented admission-control rate limiter for background readbacks per-tenant. On a small test run (Worker A + B), limiter prevented the DRAM BW from exceeding ~82GB/s and kept KV hit-rate ~75% (vs 57% uncontrolled). 99p tokens improved from 68ms to 30ms in the mixed scenario.
- Caveat: limiter increased tail for the offending short-req workload (Worker B) — but global impact on SLO-aware customers is preferable.

Open questions / risks:
- How to select thresholds safely across hardware variants (different IMC counts / NVMe bandwidths)? Needs autoscaling of thresholds per-host profile.
- Can bank-aware placement be made portable across cloud vendors? We need to evaluate allocator hooks and whether the cloud VM abstraction exposes usable bank affinity.
- Does aggressive prefetch tuning create correctness/regression risks for some model behaviors (e.g., token probability drift if we fail to prefetch some activations)? Need to check model fidelity.
- Measuring overhead: telemetry sampling at 1/100 is fine for experiments but may be too costly at high scale. Need a low-overhead detection feature for prod.

Next steps (recommended roadmap):
- Short (1-week): stabilize admission-control limiter as a runtime flag, add per-host DRAM BW telemetry to console, and roll to canary hosts behind a canary policy. Owner: Jun Park.
- Mid (3–6 weeks): prototype bank-aware allocation on a small fleet (one hardware family) and run cross-tenant placement experiments with scheduler. Owner: Riley Thompson + infra.
- Longer (quarter): integrate adaptive prefetch heuristics with Optimize (learned suggestions), add autoscaling thresholds per-host family, and expand to private deployments testing. Owner: Mei Chen + product-optimize.

Notes to self / rough TODOs:
- Add synthetic test that varies unique-read ratio and measures breakpoints for BW (script in /bench/hotset-bw).
- Add metric alert: host.memory_bandwidth_95p > host.profile_bandwidth * 0.88 AND kv_hit_rate_drop_10m > 8% -> tag as "hotset-bandwidth-coupling" in console.
- Draft a short runbook for on-call: how to pin offending tenant, enable limiter, and evict/rehydrate patterns.

Appendix: quick trace snippets (abbreviated)
- Trace: request_id=abc123 model=chat_long kv_miss_reason=evicted load_latency_ms=14.2 host_bw=93GB/s
- NVMe: read qd spike from 2 -> 18 concurrent when Worker B QPS > 420/s

Conclusion:
- We have reproducible evidence that mixed-model hotset transitions can produce bandwidth coupling that materially reduces KV cache effectiveness and increases tail latencies.
- Short-term mitigations (rate-limited backfill and scheduler placement) look promising and are low-risk. Medium-term allocator and prefetch adaptations could yield stronger improvements but require planning and cross-team effort.

If you want to run the repro locally I have the scripts and a small dataset on GCS under gs://rnw-hotset-repro/ — reach out and I’ll hand off the short checklist.
